items.title: Water bears can survive being heated, frozen, irradiated and put in space
items.claim: Tardigrades dry out into a 'tun' state and become metabolically inert. In this state they survive temperatures from near absolute zero to over 150 degrees Celsius, 1000 times the lethal radiation dose for humans, and the vacuum of space.
items.prompt: How do they survive complete desiccation?

options.text: Replacement of intracellular water with bioglasses (trehalose sugars and intrinsically disordered proteins like CAHS) that stabilise membranes and proteins in a vitrified state
Their cells contain no water in any state

items.reveal:
In favourable conditions, tardigrades are ordinary aquatic micro-animals with ~1000 cells. When their environment dries, they curl into a tun and lose 97 to 99 percent of their water.

They replace it with trehalose (a disaccharide that vitrifies on drying, forming a glass that holds membranes and proteins in place) and tardigrade-specific intrinsically disordered proteins ('CAHS' — Cytoplasmic Abundant Heat Soluble) that gel into supporting matrices.

In the tun state, metabolism stops. Without water, biochemistry can't proceed — so most chemistry that would kill the tardigrade (radiation damage requires water-radical chemistry; freezing requires ice crystal formation) is paused.

Rehydrated tardigrades resume normal life within hours. The 2007 ESA FOTON-M3 mission exposed them to open space; many survived.
items.why: Life is associated with metabolism. Some animals turn metabolism off, dehydrate to a glass-like state, and re-start later — life as a paused process.

items.title: Your core temperature varies by less than 1 degree all day
items.claim: Air temperature swings by 30 degrees C between Australian outback day and night. Sahara desert: 50 C day, 0 C night. Yet healthy human core temperature stays at 36.5-37.5 C across these extremes. We are walking thermostats.
items.prompt: How does the body hold core temperature constant?

options.text: The skin acts as insulation only

Negative feedback through the hypothalamus: sensors monitor core temperature; effectors include sweating (cooling), vasodilation/vasoconstriction (heat dump or retention), shivering (heat production), and behavioural responses (seek shade, put on clothes)
Body heat is generated constantly at the same rate

items.reveal:
The preoptic area of the hypothalamus contains warm-sensitive and cold-sensitive neurons. They integrate skin temperature (peripheral) and blood temperature (core) and adjust effector outputs.

When too hot: blood vessels in skin dilate; sweat glands release ~0.5-1.5 L/hour (up to 3 L/hour in heat-acclimated athletes); behaviour (seek shade).

When too cold: skin vessels constrict; shivering (involuntary skeletal muscle activity, heat output up to 5x resting); brown fat thermogenesis (less in adults); piloerection (goose bumps — useless on hairless humans but works in furred mammals); behaviour (seek shelter).

Fever is a deliberately raised set-point — the hypothalamus is told (by pyrogens) that 38.5 C is the new target. Your body now defends 38.5 the way it usually defends 37.

Heatstroke: thermoregulation fails at core temperatures above ~40 C. Mortality rises rapidly. Conversely, deep hypothermia (<30 C) shuts down cardiac function — but has been used surgically to extend safe ischemia times.

The set-point isn't constant: circadian variation (~0.5 C lower at night), menstrual cycle (~0.3 C higher post-ovulation), age-related decline in regulation precision.
items.why: Homeostasis is usually drawn as a circle on a board. It's an integration of dozens of mechanisms across the whole body — and breaks down in fascinating ways (fever, heatstroke, hypothermia) when stressed.

items.title: Your heart pumps 7000 litres of blood every day
items.claim: Resting heart rate ~70 bpm. Stroke volume ~70 ml. Cardiac output ~5 litres per minute, 7200 litres per day. Over an average lifetime: 250 million litres pumped — enough to fill 100 Olympic swimming pools.
items.prompt: How can such a small muscle pump so much?

options.text: The heart is hollow so volume doesn't matter

Continuous high turnover: each heartbeat moves a small volume, but ~100,000 beats per day add up; cardiac muscle is uniquely adapted (intercalated discs, dense mitochondria, near-zero anaerobic capacity) to never tire
Most of the volume is recycled within the heart
Blood is much lighter than water

items.reveal:
Cardiac muscle (myocardium) is structurally distinct from skeletal muscle. Cells are short, branching, with one or two nuclei, joined by intercalated discs containing gap junctions that synchronise contraction.

About 30% of cardiac muscle volume is mitochondria (vs 1-2% in skeletal muscle). The heart oxidises fatty acids preferentially and never fatigues under normal conditions.

It's also self-rhythmic: the sinoatrial node (in the right atrium) generates 70-80 spontaneous depolarisations per minute, propagated via the AV node and Purkinje fibres. Cut all nerves to the heart and it keeps beating (just at a different rate).

Under exercise, cardiac output can rise to 25+ L/min (5x resting) — by increasing both heart rate and stroke volume. Elite athletes have larger left ventricles and lower resting heart rates (40s, even 30s).

The heart's own coronary arteries feed it. Block one and the muscle downstream dies in minutes — myocardial infarction.
items.why: Continuous lifelong pumping sounds impossible. Heart muscle isn't ordinary muscle — it's a specialised contractile tissue evolved precisely never to stop.
